items.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: particularly Ed Berger, who’s a very dear friend and one of the most compassionate guys in the world.

ctx.x: How did you choose it? How did this album come about?

Ed Berger and Benny Carter thought that I should make one, particularly Ed Berger, who’s a very dear friend and one of the most compassionate guys in the world. He just kept saying, we’ve got to do this and we’ve got to do it, until finally we did it. Then he’s been running around like a chicken with his head cut off, pushing this thing. If you knew the amount of legwork that he’s put into it. I would have given up long ago. I would have said, “Look, Ed, let’s just play it a home and forget about it.” He has not…
What was it like to do? Is this a solo album? Or do you have a regular . . . ?

items.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998
items.q: Ed Berger had played some of it.

ctx.x: But I do think you should go home and listen to some of your own recordings.

I guess you’ve got a point there. I have some of them like this that are still in the cellophane. In fact, what recording was it, oh I did a classical album, Alec Wilder wrote a sonata for me. He had a knack of writing concerti and sonatas and things for his friends you know. And he really puts you to the test. So I recorded a thing, and I had forgotten who had written the liner notes mainly because I just glanced at them when the album came out. And it was Jim Marr had written the liner notes and we were over at…
notes — I was embarrassed. And when I got home I looked — I didn’t even realize it was Jim Marr who had written the liner notes. I didn’t tell him.
